processing: Traditionally made as a green tea: spread, fixed by heat, rolled and dried. The bitter edge of the leaf is a known problem, and some producers now spread it thinner and fix it with steam machines to tame it.
harvest_season: Picked across the growing year, and spring, summer and autumn leaf smell measurably different. As with other Chinese greens, early spring buds are the usual prize.
appearance_dry: Tight, needle-like green strips with plenty of visible white down.
appearance_liquor: Clear, pale yellow-green, sometimes faintly cloudy from the down.
appearance_wet: Tender olive-green leaves with fuzzy undersides.
taste_profile: Rich and fresh with a chestnut note and a sweet finish, firmer and more bitter than a small-leaf green if steeped hard.

brewing.notes: Glass or a porcelain gaiwan, with cooler water than you would use for a small-leaf green, because this leaf turns bitter quickly. Pull it earlier if the first cup bites.

vintage_note: Sold as a current-year tea like other Chinese greens, with early spring lots usually priced highest; drink it within a year. The same cultivar is also sold as black and white tea from Lingyun, so check which one the bag holds, and white versions are a recent line without a settled national standard.
description:
Lingyun Baihao comes from Lingyun County in the Baise area of western Guangxi, mainly around the misty Cenwang Laoshan and Qinglong mountains. The name means white down, after the thick fuzz on the underside of the leaf, and the older name Lingyun Baimao says the same thing.

The plant matters as much as the place. This is a cultivar recognised nationally in 1984, with unusually high polyphenols, reported at about 35%. That gives a strong cup, and also the bitterness that once made its green tea a hard sell beyond the region. Newer methods, including thinner spreading and steam fixing, are aimed squarely at that problem.

Expect a full, fresh green with chestnut and a sweet finish. Lab work on its aroma found linalool and geraniol among the main compounds and clear differences by season: autumn leaning minty and floral, spring fruity, summer towards citrus. Use cooler water and short steeps; most bad cups here are simply overextracted.

It is sold as a regional name protected as a geographical indication, with Lingyun producers also making black and white teas from the same leaf. Claims that it is the only cultivar in Asia suited to all six tea classes are promotional and worth ignoring. Look for plenty of down, a named harvest and the words green, black or white on the pack.
history:
The firm dates begin in the twentieth century. Lingyun tea was shown at the 1915 Panama exposition, where regional accounts credit it with a second prize, and the cultivar was recognised nationally in 1984. It appeared in Chinese tea reference books in 1994 and took a Zhongcha Cup famous tea title in 1999.

Local claims reach further back, to about three hundred years of cultivation, tribute status under the Qing and praise from emperors, but these are told as local tradition. In recent years the emphasis has shifted from green tea alone to black tea, white tea and even tea wine from the same leaf.
